hints: Think about the real size of a cell surface membrane - it is far too small to see with a light microscope and is about 7-10 thousandths of a micrometre thick, so which unit smaller than micrometres fits best?
walkthrough:
Recall Real Membrane Size**
A cell surface membrane is about 7 nm thick. That is 0.007 micrometres, so using micrometres would give a tiny awkward decimal. You and I always pick a unit that gives a sensible whole number.

Choose The Ultrastructure Unit**
For electron micrographs and membrane thickness, the standard Cambridge unit is nanometres, written as $nm$. That is $1 \times 10^{-9} m$.

hints: Look carefully at the right-hand side (B side) of Fig. 6.1 - what branching tree-like structures are attached to proteins and lipids there but are completely absent on the left-hand side?
walkthrough:
Spot The Asymmetry**
Membranes are not symmetrical. In Fig. 6.1 the left side (A side) is smooth, while the right side (B side) has many branched chains sticking out into the surroundings.

Link Sugars To Outside**
Those branched chains are carbohydrates attached to proteins to make glycoproteins and to lipids to make glycolipids, together called the glycocalyx. They are only added on the outside for cell recognition, antigens and receptors, so the side with sugars is the external surface.
Final answer: External surface has carbohydrate / sugar chains (glycocalyx) forming glycoproteins and glycolipids; no sugars on inner surface.

hints: Start with shapes - R is the tiny molecule tucked between the fatty acid tails in the hydrophobic core, while S brackets the paired heads-and-tails layer itself. What two classic fluid-mosaic components do those match?
For the tiny R molecule, think about temperature - what wedges between tails to stop them packing solid when cold and to restrain them when hot?
For the S layer, think about water - what arrangement of hydrophilic heads facing out and hydrophobic tails facing in creates a barrier?
Now link structure to permeability - why does that oily middle stop charged and polar substances crossing freely while letting small lipid-soluble substances through?
walkthrough:
Name R - Cholesterol**
R is drawn small, with a tiny head sitting among the phospholipid tails. That is cholesterol, tucked into the hydrophobic core of the bilayer.

Role Of Cholesterol**
Cholesterol fits between the fatty acid tails. At low temperatures it prevents the tails packing closely together, so it keeps fluidity. At high temperatures it restrains movement, so it stabilises the membrane. It also makes the membrane less leaky to hydrophilic / polar molecules and ions.

Name S - Phospholipid**
S brackets the double layer of heads with tails. That is the phospholipid bilayer. Remember to say phospholipid, not just lipid.

Role Of Phospholipid Bilayer**
Phospholipids arrange with hydrophilic phosphate heads facing the aqueous cytoplasm and tissue fluid, and hydrophobic fatty acid tails facing inwards away from water. This creates a continuous oily barrier. The hydrophobic core lets small lipid-soluble substances dissolve through but prevents free passage of hydrophilic / polar substances and ions, giving selective permeability.

Final answer: Component R: cholesterol; regulates / maintains fluidity and mechanical stability of membrane, reduces permeability to hydrophilic / polar substances. Component S: phospholipid; forms bilayer with hydrophilic heads facing aqueous surroundings and hydrophobic tails inside, forming a barrier to hydrophilic / polar substances.
